- Cargo vessel was approached by a small skiff carrying weapons and ladders.
What it means
UKMTO advisories of this kind are the standard early-warning format for Red Sea and Gulf of Aden traffic, and in past escalation phases they have tended to arrive in clusters: an approach report is frequently the first entry in a sequence that runs from sighting, to attempted boarding or attack, to rerouting decisions by carriers and a widening of war-risk insurance premia on the affected lane.
The detail that matters here is the kit: weapons plus ladders indicate boarding intent rather than a missile or drone profile, which points toward pirate or militia seizure attempts off the Yemeni and Somali coastlines rather than the state-backed strike campaign further north in the Bab el-Mandeb, and the two have historically repriced freight differently.
Boarding attempts near Al Mukalla sit on the eastern Gulf of Aden corridor, where incidents have on previous occasions drawn naval escort responses and pushed operators toward longer Cape routings, tightening effective vessel supply and lifting container and tanker spot rates with a lag.

October 2026 data recap
Tokens rose 37% in October
Our breakdown of the AI highlights from last month.
Tokens soared, price per token continued to fall, and agentic traffic now makes up most of what runs through OpenRouter.
Highlights
- Token volume kept rising: up 37% from September and almost 25x from January.
- Effective price per token fell: the blended average price per token kept marching down, and last month it was 57 to 70% below January averages.
- Decision models now see 21% of all requests: though the category is only weeks old, decision models now get more requests than any modality other than text models.
790 trillion tokens in October
October was the largest month in OpenRouter's history: 790T tokens, up 37% from September and a startling 25x from January.
The increase was broad based, but the refresh of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, together with the introduction of Haiku 5.5 and the rest of the Claude 5.5 family, were major contributors.
Agents consume 76% of all tokens
Agent dominance has only increased over the course of 2026.
We classify every API key as agentic, human or mixed with a weighted classifier of seven signals, including tool-call rate, number of turns and request timing.
A year ago agentic keys took 8% of tokens.
In October they took 76%, about 600T tokens.
A distinguishing feature of agentic usage is resending the same, often extensive, context on every turn, so prompt caching matters more for agents than for human usage.
Most providers served cached prefixes for 85 to 97% of agentic prompt tokens in October.
The median cache hit rate has risen steeply, from 76.1% in June to over 90% in October.
Open weights bounced back

Decision models (or System One models, in TypeSafe’s nomenclature) judge a narrow question, such as routing, moderation or a yes-or-no check.

DeepSeek fell to ninth in September and returned to second with V4.1 Flash, and InferenceNet entered the top ten at fourth.

OpenRouter crosses a 10 quadrillion annual token run rate
The AI model router's growth is being driven by autonomous agents, which now consume far more tokens than human users
OpenRouter, the platform that lets developers reach hundreds of AI models through a single API, has hit an annualized run rate of over 10 quadrillion tokens.
The milestone was announced on November 2, 2026.
The figure matters because tokens are the basic unit of AI consumption.
When usage at a middleman like OpenRouter compounds this fast, it offers a rough read on how much the broader economy is actually leaning on large language models.
The numbers behind the milestone
A token is a chunk of text, often a piece of a word, that a language model reads or writes.
Every prompt and every response gets metered in tokens, so token volume is roughly the AI industry’s version of kilowatt-hours.
OpenRouter processed approximately 194 trillion tokens in the week ending October 26, 2026.

Multiply that week by 52 and you land just over 10 quadrillion.

OpenRouter reached an annual run rate of 1.5 quadrillion tokens by May 2026.

Daily volume tells a similar story.

OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face
Sasha Blumenfeld ·
We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond.
Starting today, that extends to everyone building on Hugging Face.
Chat models on Hugging Face Inference Providers now run through OpenRouter, with the same routing across providers that OpenRouter customers already rely on.
The integration also runs the other way.
OpenRouter can now send a trace of each request to a Hugging Face Storage Bucket you own, so the prompts and responses from your real traffic sit next to the models and datasets you would use to evaluate or fine-tune on them.
The setup guide has the steps.
What you get on Hugging Face
Many chat models on Hugging Face are served by more than one provider.
OpenRouter’s provider routing now powers routing on Hugging Face Inference Providers, and it picks the provider for each request based on live price, speed, and reliability.
You don’t have to set anything up, and your existing Hugging Face token and code keep working.
You also get automatic failover.
If a provider slows down or starts failing, requests go to other providers until it recovers.
If a provider returns an error, the request is retried on the next one inside the same call.
When we rebuilt this routing in October, a live experiment measured 46% fewer requests hitting a capacity error, 16.9% faster time to first token, and 16.3% higher throughput, for 6.0% higher cost per request.
Everyone building on Hugging Face now gets the same routing.
You stay in control of the trade-off.
Adding a suffix to the model ID, such as :fastest, :cheapest, or a provider name, tells OpenRouter what to prioritize, and requests work through OpenAI’s Chat Completions and Responses APIs or Anthropic’s Messages API.
A conversation also stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache.
Each model page has a new Providers tab with live price, speed, and uptime for every provider.
You can see your spend by provider and turn off any provider you don’t want to use.
160 models from 38 labs are available this way today, which is every model OpenRouter serves that has a page on the Hub.
They include the open-weight models developers use most on OpenRouter, where open-weight models carried about 70% of paid tokens in October:
- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
- MoonshotAI Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3
- Z.ai GLM 5.3 and GLM 5.3 Flash
- Qwen3.8 27B
- MiniMax M3.1 Flash
- Xiaomi MiMo-V2.6-Flash
- NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra
- OpenAI gpt-oss-120b
Your traces can live on the Hub
Add Hugging Face Storage Buckets as a Broadcast destination (it’s in beta) and OpenRouter sends each request as a JSON file to a bucket you own.
Each file holds the input messages, the model’s output, token counts, and cost.
Images and other media are left out.
That’s the raw material for an evaluation set or a fine-tuning run on an open-weight model.
You can organize the files by date or by API key.
Get started
On Hugging Face:
- Create a token at hf.co/settings/tokens with the “Make calls to Inference Providers” permission.
- Open any supported model’s page on the Hub.
Chat with it there, or click View code for setup steps for your code or your coding agent, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and Hermes A

Our platform delivers a thorough analysis of cryptocurrency Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF) landscape, featuring a wide range of metrics including daily net inflows and outflows, cumulative total Net Inflow, trading volumes, and the total assets.
It goes further by offering an in-depth multi-indicator comparison for each specific Bitcoin ETF, such as the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust (GBTC), Fidelity's Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), and BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), among others.
This comparison is enriched with historical data, which is presented through detailed visual charts, ensuring a comprehensive and coherent overview of the ETF market's dynamics.
Furthermore, our service extends to include the latest ETF News, offering timely updates and insights into developments within the ETF sector, ensuring that investors stay informed on the most recent events and announcements.
Additionally, we provide a detailed Spot ETF Schedule, facilitating a forward-looking view into the market by detailing upcoming listings, regulatory decisions, and other critical dates pertinent to Bitcoin ETFs.
This combination of real-time news updates and a comprehensive schedule offers a holistic view of the market, aiding investors in making informed decisions.
A Bitcoin Spot ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund) is a type of investment fund that aims to track the actual ("spot") price of Bitcoin, the leading cryptocurrency, and is traded on traditional stock exchanges.
Unlike Bitcoin futures ETFs, which are based on contracts to buy or sell cryptocurrency at a future date, a spot ETF would be backed by actual Bitcoin holdings.
This means that the ETF would purchase and hold Bitcoin directly, allowing investors to gain exposure to the price movements of Bitcoin without having to buy, store, and secure cryptocurrency themselves.
Our platform provides an exhaustive analysis of the Bitcoin ETF market by meticulously monitoring a curated list of ten Bitcoin ETFs, offering a comprehensive view of the sector.
The selection encompasses notable funds such as Grayscale's Bitcoin ETF(GBTC), Fidelity's Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), and BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), alongside others including Franklin Templeton Digital Holdings Trust (EZBC), ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF (ARKB), VanEck Bitcoin ETF (HODL), Invesco Galaxy Bitcoin ETF (BTCO), Valkyrie Bitcoin Fund (BRRR), WisdomTree Bitcoin Trust (BTCW), and Bitwise Bitcoin ETF (BITB).

We will cover key Ethereum ETFs like VanEck Ethereum ETF, ARK 21Shares Ethereum ETF, Hashdex Nasdaq Ethereum ETF, Grayscale Ethereum Trust Conversion (ETHE), Invesco Galaxy Ethereum ETF, iShares Ethereum Trust, and Fidelity Ethereum Fund.
